idea: In graphics, nearly every quantity that matters — a pixel's color, a surface's charge, a fluid's flow — comes from an infinity of tiny contributions arriving from all directions and times at once. Light is the prime example: a single point on your screen receives photons from countless paths through the scene, scattered by materials, bouncing off surfaces, arriving over a continuous spectrum of directions. The pixel's final color is literally the sum of all those contributions. But you cannot enumerate an infinite sum. The core insight is that you never need to: most of the contribution is concentrated in a few large peaks. By breaking the infinite total into finite chunks — sampling along rays, discretizing time, chopping space into voxels — you can add up the chunks and trust that as you make the chunks smaller, your finite sum closes in on the true infinite answer. This is integration: turning an uncountable infinity into a countable approximation.
why: Integration works because continuous quantities are not random and scattered; they have structure. Most of the contribution comes from regions of high density — where light is bright, where mass clusters, where forces concentrate — and these regions are finite in number and size. The guarantees come from the mathematics: any continuous total can be trapped between an over-estimate and an under-estimate (by summing tall and short rectangles under a curve), and as you chop your intervals thinner, both traps squeeze tighter and tighter toward the true answer. This squeezing never stops — you can always get closer — but you reach the 'close enough' point long before infinity. The method fails only when the quantity has wild, unbounded spikes (infinite variance), but in graphics, real physics forces smoothness: light refracts gradually, materials blend, heat diffuses. The structure of physics itself guarantees that your approximation converges.
dots: Across these 16 papers, integration appears in disguises that all share one move: formulate the answer as a continuous sum, then approximate it with samples or pieces. In volumetric rendering (GenPIE, Sample Matching, Efficient Fur), light traveling through smoke or fog is a ray integral — light lost to scattering plus light arriving from all directions — broken into small segments along the ray, evaluated stochastically. In holography (HoloPathTracer), the wavefront is an integral over all light paths; Monte Carlo path tracing randomly samples paths and weights them to approximate this path integral. In inverse problems (Thermal Non-Line-of-Sight, Gradient Domain Reconstruction), the forward model is an integral (convolution of light transport with a kernel, or a Poisson integral); the solver inverts this by treating it as an optimization over gradients or learned features, then reconstructs. In numerical PDEs (Schrödinger Bridges, Biharmonic Diffusion), the solution satisfies a differential equation (which locally sums up small changes); the solver samples random walks or boundary conditions to estimate the integral form. In imaging (Hi-SPAD, Hyperspectral), photon arrivals are random samples; their histogram is the integral of the spectrum. In geometry (Antipodal Winding Numbers), point-in-shape tests use boundary integrals expressed as ray-surface intersections; the method transforms the volume integral into a surface integral, which is far cheaper to compute. In differentiable rendering (Closed-Form Convolution, Differentiable Neutron Transport), you need the derivative of an integral; by sampling the integrand or using convolution, you can backpropagation through the sum. The single thread: pick the right decomposition of your integral, evaluate it piecewise, and sum.
picture: Imagine sunlight hitting a table. The table's color is not determined by just the one ray of sunlight coming straight down from the sun — it is the sum of light arriving from every angle: bounced off clouds, reflected from nearby walls, scattered by the air itself, each contributing a tiny bit to the final brightness you see. You cannot measure each of those infinite directions separately, so instead you point a light meter in a few key directions, measure in each, and add them up. The more directions you measure, the closer your sum gets to the true total. By noon tomorrow, when you have sampled more directions and time has smoothed out the variations, your sum will be almost exact. This is exactly what a rendering algorithm does: sample the light from many directions and times along a ray, add them up, and trust that enough samples will converge to the true color.
